Week 83 Appendix: The Attorney General's Refusal

An admission of non-independence at the Justice Department opened a week of self-dealing, deportation courts, and press retaliation, checked narrowly by courts.

This week showed a consolidating pattern of executive impunity coupled with visible institutional friction. The Attorney General's public refusal to pledge DOJ independence, continued mass deportation courts denying due process, and DOJ efforts to reinstate dismissed prosecutions (Ábrego García) illustrate a Justice Department increasingly organized around presidential will rather than neutral law enforcement. Simultaneously, self-dealing reached new heights: a Trump-family crypto venture received a federal bank charter from a Trump-appointed regulator, Treasury quietly destroyed anti-money-laundering beneficial-ownership data, and the president sold early access to market-moving Truth Social posts. Press freedom faced direct assault—ABC/Disney sued the FCC over alleged retaliatory licensing, Pentagon fired Stars and Stripes journalists for covering ship conditions, and the White House publicly attacked a CNN reporter and her children. Foreign policy showed erratic, personalist decision-making (threatening to bomb an ally, unilaterally declaring intent to annex the Strait of Hormuz, cutting South Korea exercises based on rapport with Kim Jong Un). Courts and states pushed back meaningfully, including SCOTUS denying Trump's Carroll appeal, a Fourth Circuit religious-freedom ruling limiting ICE at churches, and DHS's dramatic walk-back of inflated noncitizen voter fraud claims.
